newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen opening higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen opening higher.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to move higher at the start of trading Thursday, and investors will be watching for the techs to follow through on yesterday's rally.
Volume will thin out during the day as market players head home for the three-day Good Friday/Easter weekend.

"We had a decent day yesterday, and, if the techs continue doing well, the market will move higher. I don't think jobless claims will affect bonds unless they are unusually strong," said Hildergard Zagorski, analyst at Prudential Securities.
Jobless claims for the week ended March 22 are expected to come in at 313,000, up from the previous week's 312,000.
February existing home sales are expected to climb to 4.05 million from the previous month's 3.94 million.

"Any data which may surprise the market in terms of the strength of the economy will keep up the pressure as to when the next interest rate hike is coming," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
"High technology stocks which did well yesterday will probably continue to trade higher today. The momentum was pretty strong."

Tokyo stocks ended sharply lower on Thursday, jolted by a fall in bank shares triggered by news that Nippon Credit Bank Ltd is working out a restructuring plan which may include the sale of its main office in Tokyo.
The Nikkei Average closed 262.03 points, or 1.42 percent, down at 18,210.42.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 23.3 at 4324.8.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, International Business Machines Corp, which rose 4-1/2 on Wednesday, was up 1/4 at 140-7/8, while Digital Equipment Corp added 1/8 at 29-1/2.

Motorola Inc, another big gainer on Wednesday, was down one at 61 after the company said that it expected a year-on-year decline in quarterly earnings to persist until later this year, despite a modest recovery in its key semiconductor business.

Philip Morris Cos Inc shares slipped 1/2 to 118-7/8 after news that a Mississippi judge had ruled that internal documents from Brooke Group could be turned over to plaintiffs. The dollar was weak in late Tokyo trading and
dipped against the mark and yen in Europe.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that if all goes according to plan, the nation's biggest provider of variable annuities is about to grow stronger still.

Next month, the American Association of Retired Persons will begin marketing a variable annuity product underwritten by Hartford Life, a unit of ITT Hartford Group designed specifically for the AARP's 33 million members.
The New York Times Market Place writes that now that the Federal Reserve has raised its short-term interest rates, Wall Street is turning its focus again to corporate earnings.
